title: Diagnosis of Hymenoptera Venom Allergy: State of the Art, Challenges, and Perspectives
main_conclusion: The diagnosis of Hymenoptera venom allergy, the leading cause of anaphylaxis in adults, remains challenging despite advances in molecular diagnostics. Current methods face limitations such as double positivity of specific IgE to honeybee and wasp venom due to cross-reactive carbohydrate determinants. The review underscores the need for novel diagnostic approaches, including multidimensional molecular analyses, to improve accuracy and enable personalized venom immunotherapy.
narrative_summary: Hymenoptera venom allergy is a common cause of anaphylaxis, particularly in adults, and proper diagnosis is essential for guiding venom immunotherapy, which significantly reduces the risk of severe reactions. Diagnosis begins with clinical history and identification of the stinging insect, but patient and physician errors in insect recognition are common. The main diagnostic tools are skin tests and measurement of venom-specific IgE antibodies, though both have limitations. A major challenge is double positivity for honeybee and wasp venom IgE, often due to cross-reactive carbohydrate determinants (CCDs) rather than true dual sensitization. Molecular diagnostics using recombinant allergens can help distinguish genuine sensitivities from cross-reactivity. The basophil activation test, while more specific, is not widely available and may also be affected by CCDs. Recent proteomic and metabolomic studies have identified potential biomarkers for venom allergy, offering hope for improved diagnostics. The review highlights the need for standardized, accessible, and more precise diagnostic tests to overcome current challenges and ensure appropriate patient management. Ultimately, accurate diagnosis is the cornerstone of effective venom immunotherapy and prevention of life-threatening anaphylaxis.
clinical_background: Hymenoptera venom allergy represents the leading cause of anaphylaxis among adults and the second most common in children. Stings can provoke reactions ranging from normal local responses to large local reactions and systemic manifestations involving the skin, respiratory tract, cardiovascular system, gastrointestinal tract, or nervous system. European epidemiological data indicate that systemic reactions occur in 0.3 to 8.9% of adults and up to 32% of beekeepers. Although fatalities are uncommon, Hymenoptera stings account for 20% of anaphylaxis-related deaths. Thus, this allergy is potentially life-threatening, and all patients with systemic symptoms require thorough diagnostic evaluation. Accurate diagnosis is essential for appropriate management, including venom immunotherapy (VIT), which is the most effective treatment for reducing the risk of future severe reactions and for improving quality of life. Currently, improved diagnostic tools enable individualized diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.
